PHSCS 587

Drift, mobility and conductivity

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how carrier sign and scattering determine drift current

An electric field changes carrier momentum between scattering events. In the low-field regime, electron drift velocity is vn = −μnEfield and hole drift velocity is vp = +μpEfield. Positive mobilities μn and μp have units m²/(V·s), or cm²/(V·s) with consistent concentrations and lengths. Thermal motion can be rapid even when its directional average vanishes.

Conventional current includes the charge sign: Jn,drift = qnμnEfield and Jp,drift = qpμpEfield. Both drift currents point along the electric field. Total conductivity is σ = q(nμn + pμp), in S/m in SI. In a simple isotropic relaxation-time model, μ = qτm/m*, where τm is a momentum-relaxation time and m* is the transport mass.

Lattice vibrations, ionized impurities, interfaces and other processes scatter carriers. Their relative importance changes with temperature, doping and structure, so a single temperature trend for mobility is insufficient. At strong fields, carrier heating and scattering make average drift speed depart from μE and tend toward a material-dependent saturation scale. This microscopic velocity saturation differs from a MOSFET’s channel-electrostatic current saturation, although both can influence its I–V curve.

Example

If electron density stays fixed while a change in scattering halves μn, the electron contribution to conductivity halves. A simultaneous change in density would need to be counted separately.

Practice

1. Which way is the conventional electron drift current relative to electron drift velocity?

Multiply particle flux by charge −q.

They point in opposite directions. Electrons drift against the field, while their conventional drift current points along it.
